experiments.title: The Balloon That Clings to a Wall
experiments.description: Can an ordinary balloon stay on a wall without glue? Change one variable and record how long it clings.
experiments.principle: Frictional contact transfers charge between some materials. A charged balloon polarizes the nearby wall surface, creating an electrostatic attraction.
steps: Rub the balloon against wool for five strokes.
Gently place the rubbed side against the wall and release it.
Measure how many seconds it remains on the wall.
Repeat with ten strokes, keeping other conditions similar. Compare the times.
experiments.safety: Keep loose balloon pieces away from young children; avoid latex if allergic.

story.title: The Wall That Held a Secret
story.body: In a quiet classroom, a balloon appeared to defy gravity. Oracle asked the students to count the rubs and time what happened. They soon discovered that careful measurements can turn a surprise into an experiment.

experiments.title: Pendulum: Does Length Change the Rhythm?
experiments.description: Build two simple pendulums and measure how length affects their swing time.
experiments.principle: For a small-angle simple pendulum, the period grows approximately with the square root of its length. The bob mass has little effect under ideal conditions.
steps: Tie one washer to a 30 cm string on a stable support.
Pull it aside by a small angle and release without pushing.
Time ten complete swings; divide by ten.
Repeat at 60 cm length, keeping the release angle and washer the same.
experiments.safety: Use small, lightweight washers, keep the swinging path clear, and avoid overhead installation.

story.title: The Clockmaker’s Two Strings
story.body: Ada had two clocks that never quite agreed. She tested the lengths of their pendulums, wrote down ten swings at a time, and found a rule hidden in their rhythm.

experiments.title: Where Do the Rainbow Colors Hide?
experiments.description: Make a miniature spectrum from daylight and observe how color separates.
experiments.principle: White light includes many visible wavelengths. Refraction and internal reflection in water can separate colors into a spectrum.
steps: Put a shallow layer of water in the tray.
Set the small mirror partly into the water at an angle.
Aim daylight onto the mirror so reflected light falls onto white paper.
Adjust the paper and mirror until you find colors; record the order.
experiments.safety: Never look directly at the Sun or aim focused reflections into eyes. Use only daylight, not lasers.

sources.label: Science Buddies · How Many Colors in a Rainbow?

story.title: Seven Colors at the Window
story.body: When daylight struck the water, a quiet wall became a little theater of colors. Oracle asked which color appeared first and why the white beam had changed.

experiments.title: Walking Water Without Lifting the Cup
experiments.description: Can water climb paper and move into a neighboring cup?
experiments.principle: Capillary action carries water through tiny pores in paper towels. Adhesion, cohesion and surface tension contribute to this transport.
steps: Fill one cup halfway and leave the second empty.
Fold the towel into a narrow strip.
Place one end in the water and the other in the empty cup.
Check every 15 minutes and record water levels.
experiments.safety: Place cups on a spill-proof tray. Do not drink the experimental water.

story.title: A Bridge Made of Paper
story.body: Professor Willow forbade the students from moving either cup. Instead of lifting the water, they gave it a path, and watched the bridge slowly do the work.

experiments.title: Paper Airplane: A Study in Drag
experiments.description: Measure how a small wing change affects distance rather than guessing which plane is fastest.
experiments.principle: Drag is the air resistance opposite the direction of motion. Changing wing flaps can increase drag and alter a paper aircraft’s flight.
materials: Tape to mark a start line
steps: Fold two matching paper airplanes.
Throw the first five times from the same line, recording distance.
Fold small symmetric flaps up on the second plane.
Throw five times using the same technique and compare average distances.
experiments.safety: Keep the test lane free of people; do not point planes toward faces.

sources.label: Science Buddies · Paper Airplanes and Aerodynamics

story.title: The Plane That Wouldn’t Race
story.body: Captain Nova liked sleek designs, but a simple paper wing challenged every assumption. Five flights later, measurements beat the captain’s favorite guess.

experiments.title: How Small Gaps Lift Water
experiments.description: Compare how far water travels between nearby surfaces, and what happens when the space narrows.
experiments.principle: Capillary rise is stronger in narrower wettable gaps because the interaction of surface tension and adhesion with geometry can counteract gravity.
steps: Place spacers between the strips and hold them together loosely with a rubber band.
Dip the bottom edge into a shallow tray of colored water.
Observe the water level.
Move one spacer away to make a tapered gap, then compare water levels in wide and narrow regions.
experiments.safety: Use plastic strips rather than glass to avoid cuts; clean up spills.

story.title: The Water That Climbed
story.body: The student could not explain why the water rose higher in the tiniest gap. A second test with a wider gap supplied the missing evidence, and the puzzle opened up.
